title: Genuina principia doctrinae de statu aequilibrii et motu corporum tam perfecte flesibilium quam elasticorum

deep.reconstruction:
The page finishes Euler's classification of planar elastic curves (elasticae) from his general equilibrium method, then turns to dynamics. From the previous page, the radius of curvature as a function of the tangent angle φ is r = a/√(4n+1−4n cos φ) = a/√(1+8n sin²(φ/2)). Equivalently the curvature is 1/r = √(1+8n sin²(φ/2))/a, or κ² = (1+4n−4n cos φ)/a². This is the standard first integral of the elastica, κ²/2 = λ cos φ + C. Combined with x = a²/(2nr) − a/(2n), it gives curvature linear in the abscissa x, i.e. bending moment proportional to the lever arm of the end load. Euler says this property should be noted as common to all elasticae.

The case analysis splits on the sign and size of 8n:
(i) 8n = m > 0: the radical is always real, so φ grows without bound. This is the non-inflectional (orbit-like) elastica with no zero of curvature.
(ii) 8n = 0: a circle, r = a.
(iii) 8n = −m with 0 < m < 1: √(1 − m sin²(φ/2)) is still real for all φ, so this is again a non-inflectional family.
(iv) m = 1: the curvature becomes cos(φ/2)/a, which vanishes at φ = π. This is the limiting (separatrix) elastica, whose tangent turns asymptotically and which approaches a straight asymptote.
(v) m > 1: reality requires sin²(φ/2) < 1/m. The amplitude is bounded, giving the inflectional elasticae, i.e. the periodic wavy forms of the buckled rod.
Euler refers these species back to the Additamentum 'De curvis elasticis' of the Methodus inveniendi (1744), his 'Tractatus de Problemate Isoperimetrico'.

§XXXIV declines further equilibrium examples as already abundantly treated elsewhere. It claims the method's advantage is uniformity across all kinds of flexible and elastic bodies, and announces that the second part applies the same method to motion.

'Problema generale alterum' then poses the problem: for a perfectly flexible or elastic thread acted on by arbitrary forces and moving arbitrarily, set out the principles that determine the motion. The next page restricts to planar motion and makes φ a function of the two variables s and t. This leads into partial differential equations.
errors: For m = 1 (8n = −1) the printed text gives r = a cos ½φ. From r = a/√(1 − sin²(φ/2)) one gets r = a/cos ½φ; it is the curvature 1/r that equals cos(½φ)/a. The printed formula inverts the relation (misprint or slip).

Minor gap: for m = 1 Euler says φ can still run through all values. In fact the separatrix elastica reaches φ = π only asymptotically, after infinite arc length, so φ ranges over (−π, π) rather than all values.

ideas.what: Intrinsic (curvature vs tangent-angle) equation of the elastica, r = a/√(1+8n sin²½φ), and its classification by the parameter into non-inflectional, circular, separatrix and inflectional species.
ideas.modern_name: Classification of Euler's elastica via the pendulum analogy / elliptic modulus (rotating vs separatrix vs oscillating regimes)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler 1744 (Methodus inveniendi, Additamentum I); pendulum analogy made explicit by Kirchhoff 1859
ideas.where_published: E65 Methodus inveniendi (1744), Additamentum I De curvis elasticis

ideas.what: Curvature of the elastica is linear in the abscissa (bending moment proportional to lever arm), noted as common to all elasticae.
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Bernoulli bending law (moment ∝ curvature) for an end-loaded rod
ideas.usually_credited_to: Jakob Bernoulli (1694), Daniel Bernoulli and Euler (1744)
ideas.where_published: E65 Additamentum I; Jakob Bernoulli's papers on the elastica

ideas.what: Posing the general dynamics of a flexible or elastic filament in the plane, with the tangent angle a function of arc length and time.
ideas.modern_name: Planar dynamics of strings and rods (Kirchhoff-rod / inextensible-string PDEs in intrinsic coordinates)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler, d'Alembert, D. Bernoulli (1740s–1770s); Truesdell's 'Rational mechanics of flexible or elastic bodies' discusses E410
ideas.where_published: E410 itself, discussed in Truesdell, Opera Omnia II 11₂ (1960)

deep.surprise_reason: This page summarizes Euler's well-known 1744 elastica classification and transitions to the dynamics part of E410, which Truesdell analysed thoroughly. The only notable item is the r = a cos ½φ slip.
transcription_corrections: The transcription uses Φ on this page and φ elsewhere; it is the same tangent angle φ throughout.
'sin ½Φ²' means sin²(½φ) in Euler's notation.
